paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: One of Mark Smith's final acts in his corporate life was sending off an email to his then employer outlining how the company was not, in his opinion, serving its customers and stating his intention to set up his own business. Statistics show that this was a high-stakes decision. In the USA and UK just over 50% of business start-ups cease operation within two years. In New Zealand the rate is even higher with about 60% going out of business. So when Smith resigned the following week, leaving behind a $150,000 salary and started a new life in business for himself-in rubbish removal-he was taking a big chance.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Nonetheless, there's still no shortage of would-be entrepreneurs like Smith lining up to put their ideas, and financial security, on the line. Last year, for the first time, the total number of small businesses in New Zealand-those with up to 19 staff-topped 500,000. So what's the key to making it work? Andy Hamilton, an independent business advisor, challenges would-be entrepreneurs to address seven really difficult issues, about their timing, market, product and so on. 'The reality is most people starting a business don't want to know the truth,' says Hamilton. What's more, he believes that too often emotion gets in the way.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Whatever your business idea, the only guarantee is that success will not be straightforward. 'If you reckon it's going to be easy doing a start-up, you are in for a major shock,' says Hamilton. 'It's a 10-year commitment and ... the consequences for family life are pretty massive.' One definition of an entrepreneur is someone who will work 80 hours a week to avoid working 40 in a corporation. Research has also revealed that start-up owners were 'significantly less satisfied' with their work-life balance than other small-to medium enterprise owners, reflecting the long hours necessary, particularly in the early years.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Business owner Wendy Kerr, author of Corporate Crossovers, interviewed 300 women who ran their own businesses and found a range of motivations for going out on their own. New business advisor Liz Wotherspoon takes up the point. 'I'm sure there are examples of people whose plan has always been to run their own show and their time in a corporate was a means to an end,' she says. But there are other people, Wotherspoon continues, who may have become dissatisfied in the hierarchy or been made redundant, or whose decision has in some way been forced on them by changes to the organisation for which they worked.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: One of the biggest issues for new entrepreneurs, of course, is funding, and the reserves they'll need as a buffer against months of no or very low income. Estimates of how much is enough vary, but based on the women she interviewed, Kerr suggests eight months. With that security, she believes, they weren't waking up at 3 am worrying about how they were going to pay the mortgage. However, although struggling new business owners frequently cite lack of money as the reason for their early problems, Hamilton argues there's more to it. 'It's lack of sales, and that's not the same thing... Sales trump everything.'

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Another issue is that new business owners operate outside their area of expertise. They're attempting to be all things to all people, from the managing director to the delivery driver, because they can't afford to hire. Auckland business coach Fiona Clark recommends her clients tap into a network of advisors who can be taken on for short periods when they are required, from human resources specialists to social media experts. 'People are wearing too many hats, trying to do it all, 'she says. Clark explains that owners feel obliged to do everything but they have to realise that this simply isn't possible.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Diane Stanbra got her idea for a new business after touring a new waterfront development in Auckland. One of the plans was for people to be able to sit on the grass after dark to enjoy a movie. Wouldn't it be great, she thought, if they could eat a picnic at the same time. With a full-time job at a software corporation, she had to work on the idea in her own time. OOn the first night, she produced eighty $15 picnic boxes and sold less than twenty. It might have been demoralising, but Stanbra says the feedback was overwhelmingly positive. It gave her the determination to carry on with the idea over that first unpredictable summer, during which the weather restricted trading to just nine days. She then took the sensible step of speaking to a business advisor at her bank. On the basis of this discussion, she raised her price to $25 and contracted a highly-regarded chef from the restaurant world to take over food preparation. Three years later, sales had reached a point where she could give up her other job and concentrate on growing the business. In the year after she went full-time, turnover increased nearly 200%, with weddings being a secondary growth area. These figures helped her win an award for best emerging small business.
